Production for the rest of 2026 is expected to remain largely unaffected
[KUALA LUMPUR] Malaysia’s SD Guthrie, one of the world’s largest palm oil producers, said on Tuesday (Aug 11) that it expects production to be impacted in 2027 and 2028 with El Niño set to bring drier and hotter weather.
Production for the rest of 2026 is expected to remain largely unaffected by El Niño, as its effects are not felt immediately but instead follow a 12-to-16-month lag, chief executive officer Mohd Haris Mohd Arshad said at a press conference.
SD Guthrie posted a net profit of RM987 million (US$241.3 million) for the April-June period, almost double the RM505 million from a year earlier.
However, its revenue declined to RM4.94 billion from RM5.17 billion.
The company – based in Kuala Lumpur with operations in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Solomon Islands – saw its shares fall 0.9 per cent to RM6.77 as of 0645 GMT.
In a statement on its second-quarter results, SD Guthrie said its performance was underpinned by gains from its industrial development and downstream segment. That helped offset the decline from its upstream business, which was partly cushioned by higher average crude palm oil (CPO) and palm kernel prices.
In the near-to-medium term, tightening global supplies and resilient demand are expected to keep CPO prices elevated, the company said.
“Supply-side pressures are likely to intensify with the anticipated emergence of El Niño conditions towards the end of the year, while demand will be underpinned by the implementation of Indonesia’s B50 biodiesel mandate and firm crude oil prices amid renewed geopolitical tensions,” it said.
Malaysia’s benchmark CPO prices have climbed 18 per cent to RM4,723 a metric ton so far this year.
CPO prices are expected to range between RM4,600 and RM5,000 over the remainder of this year, before potentially rising to RM5,200 in the first quarter of next year, Sandeep Bhan, SD Guthrie’s global trading CEO, said at the press briefing. REUTERS

sources.news_title: Assessing the Global Temperature and Precipitation in July 2026
sources.text:
July 2026 tied for the warmest July on record, globally, and ocean surface temperature reached a record high for July
July Highlights:
- The globe tied with 2024 as the warmest July on record, driven by record-warm oceans and above-average land temperatures.
- Across the globe, areas with record-high July temperatures were widespread, spanning across portions of most continents and every major ocean basin.
- The global sea ice extent was the fourth lowest for July on record.
- Globally, July featured nine tropical storms, which is near average for the month.
Temperature
Global surface temperatures in July 2026 were 2.12°F (1.18°C) above the 20th-century average, tying with 2024 for the warmest July on record. The past four Julys (2023–26) were the four warmest on record, with 2023, 2024, and 2026 each having a July temperature departure that exceeded +1.8°F (+1.0°C). This month also marked the 55th-consecutive July with a global temperature departure above the 20th-century average; the most recent below-average July occurred in 1971.
Warmer-than-average conditions dominated across much of the globe in July 2026. Notable temperature departures of +3.6°F (+2.0°C) or higher occurred across much of the land surfaces, specifically North and South America, western Europe, central Africa, a broad swath of Asia and central Antarctica. Averaged as a whole, the global land surface came in at third highest on record for July. The Northern Hemisphere land set an all-time July record, surpassing the previous 2024 record. The Southern Hemisphere land temperature was warmer-than-normal, but finished outside the top 10. In addition to land surfaces, the north and the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean also had temperature departures exceeding +3.6°F (+2.0°C). Record-high July temperatures were widespread, spanning the British Isles, western Europe, the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, and portions across North and South America, Africa, Asia, the Arctic and parts of every major ocean basin.
The global ocean temperature was the highest on record for the month at 1.84°F (1.02°C), with 2026 marking the first July to surpass +1.8°F (1.0°C). The global ocean temperature departure for July tied with August and September 2023 as the third-highest monthly departure for any month on record, trailing behind the tied record-holders of January and February 2024. Notably, all of these top-ranking monthly global ocean temperature departures occurred during an El Niño episode.
Below-average temperatures were observed in Alaska, northern and eastern Europe, much of Antarctica, far northern Canada, the southern tip of South America and far eastern Russia. Record-cold temperature departures were rare, limited to a small area in Antarctica. No other land or ocean regions experienced record-low July temperatures.
Regionally, most continents and regions recorded a top-10 warm July. North America, Africa, and Asia experienced their warmest July on record, followed by the Arctic (third warmest), South America (sixth warmest), Europe (tied for seventh warmest) and Oceania (eighth warmest). Antarctica was the only region with below-average July temperatures—Antarctica’s coldest July since 2016.
Year-to-date
Looking at the year-to-date, the January–July global surface temperature was third highest on record. According to NCEI’s Global Annual Temperature Outlook, it is very likely that 2026 will rank among the five-warmest years on record, with the highest probabilities favoring it as the third- or fourth-warmest year on record. According to NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean during July 2026 and is expected to strengthen through the end of the year. If El Niño continues to intensify, it could drive global temperatures even higher, potentially pushing 2026 into an even warmer final ranking.
Sea Ice
Global sea ice extent was the fourth smallest for July in the 48-year record, averaging 8.77 million square miles, which is 810,000 square miles below the 1991–2020 average. The Arctic fell 400,000 square miles below average—the sixth-lowest July extent on record. Meanwhile, Antarctic sea ice was 410,000 square miles below average, ranking as the fifth-smallest July extent.
Tropical Cyclones
Globally, July featured nine tropical storms, which is near average for the month. Five of those reached tropical cyclone strength and three reached major tropical cyclone strength. The number of named storms was near normal across the primary active basins: the Atlantic (one tropical storm), East Pacific (four named storms, including two hurricanes) and West Pacific basins (four named storms, including three typhoons). All three Category 5 storms occurred in the Pacific Ocean, while no storms developed in any other basin.
In the Atlantic, Tropical Storm Bertha—the basin’s sole named storm—brought strong winds, coastal flooding and heavy rainfall to parts of the U.S. Gulf Coast before making landfall in southeastern Louisiana. In the East Pacific, Category 5 Hurricane Genevieve generated swells and rip currents along parts of Mexico and Baja California, though it remained offshore and never made landfall. In the West Pacific, Super Typhoon Bavi reached Category 5-equivalent intensity, affecting the Mariana Islands before delivering destructive winds and heavy rainfall to parts of eastern and southeastern Asia.
For a more complete summary of climate conditions and events, see our July 2026 Global Climate Report or explore our Climate at a Glance Global Time Series.

10 Aug 2026 El Niño and the fight over what it means
Meteorologists expect the El Niño now building in the Pacific Ocean to be the strongest on record, peaking between September and December. This recurring warming of surface ocean waters occurs irregularly every two to seven years, temporarily raising global temperatures and reshaping rainfall worldwide.
The UN World Food Programme estimates the El Niño on the horizon could push, at minimum, 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027 – across 45 countries already struggling to feed their populations, with the sharpest increases in Central America and Southern Africa.
In South Asia, new research shows that global warming is strengthening the link between El Niño and drought in India. In Latin America, maize and bean harvests may fail in fragile parts of Nicaragua, and irrigated crops in Colombia and northeastern Brazil will most likely face water restrictions. This impacts food security further away as well; the EU imports close to 190 billion Euro of food a year from the regions most exposed. And in Europe directly, low river flows threaten hydropower and agriculture.
Those are the numbers. What concerns us at WACC just as much, however, is the story that will be told about the numbers – and how that story might affect action on climate change.
As much of the media coverage of the issue explains, El Niño is a natural cycle. However, scientists are clear that this year’s fires and heatwaves, especially in the Northern Hemisphere, are driven by fossil fuel emissions, not by El Niño, which only adds perhaps a tenth or two of a degree to a long-term warming trend.
This is creating fertile ground for disinformation campaigns seeking to deny or minimize climate change. Most advance the notion that the extreme weather events we are experiencing are a naturally occurring phenomenon and not caused by human activity.
This pattern is already visible. When Europe’s record heatwave arrived in June, social media filled with claims that the temperatures were nothing unusual, citing London heatwaves from the 1970s. After the 2024 floods in eastern Spain that killed more than 230 people, false claims spread that dams had been deliberately dismantled and that European river restoration rules caused the disaster, disinformation amplified by far-right Vox politicians.
Disinformation is not a naturally occurring phenomenon but “a tactic” the powerful use to defend the status quo, notes Philip Newell of the Climate Action Against Disinformation (CAAD) network. It appears however, that the tactic has shifted.
Outright denial has largely given way to attacks on climate policy itself, amplified by generative AI and spiking whenever a heatwave, flood, or drought makes the news – which is precisely when affected communities need trustworthy information the most.
This is precisely why democratic and people-centred communication and information ecosystems, especially at the local level, are vital climate stability infrastructures that protect us all, not an optional extra.
Our partners across the world show what that looks like. For example:
- Grupo COMUNICARTE has spent decades among the people in Colombia’s high-altitude Andean páramos ecosystem, weaving conservation into local recipes, elders’ stories, and mountain legends until protection became something communities owned rather than something imposed by the authorities.
- Nepal’s Indigenous Rights Foundation broadcasts dialogues between Indigenous communities, government officials, and hydropower developers, reaching roughly a million people and making decision-makers publicly accountable.
- In the Niger Delta in Nigeria, the Media Awareness and Justice Initiative helps communities collect their own environmental data, turning complaints dismissed as anecdotal into evidence-backed reports.
None of these interventions are fact-checking operations, which is how disinformation tends to be tackled. Rather, these initiatives do something that is both more difficult and more durable – they build trust, they treat farmers and elders as knowledge holders alongside scientists, and they keep local narratives at the centre.
Disinformation struggles in places where people already know whom to believe.
At the UN climate change conference COP30 last November, 12 governments signed a first-ever “Declaration on Information Integrity on Climate Change,” promising what Brazil’s president, João Brant, called “a wave of truth.”
This is a welcome development. However, in most of the places El Niño will hit hardest, the key channels informing communities and fighting disinformation – community radio stations, Indigenous media networks, and local journalists – work on very little.
Funding, supporting, and protecting them is not charity nor is it optional. It is climate action.

NOAA releases updated 2026 Atlantic hurricane outlook as looming 'Super' El Niño aims to limit activity
Government forecasters cautioned that a record-breaking El Niño event could produce atmospheric impacts never before seen.
NOAA maintained its forecast for a below-average Atlantic hurricane season, the agency announced in its final 2026 hurricane season outlook Thursday. Government forecasters said they expect a very strong El Niño climate pattern to last through this fall, creating atmospheric conditions that will suppress tropical development in the Atlantic Ocean.
LATEST FROM FOX WEATHER HURRICANE SPECIALIST BRYAN NORCROSS
The agency expects 7 to 13 named storms, 2 to 6 hurricanes, including 0 to 2 major (Category 3 or stronger) hurricanes. Those ranges include Tropical Storms Arthur and Bertha, which formed in the Gulf earlier this summer.
This is a slight reduction from NOAA's initial forecast that was issued in late May, which called for a below-average season with 8 to 14 named storms, 3 to 6 hurricanes, including 1 to 3 major hurricanes.
In comparison, an average Atlantic hurricane season produces 14 named storms, including 7 hurricanes and 3 major hurricanes.
NOAA also raised the probability of a below-average season from 55% to 75%.
"If the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season ends up being below-normal, it would mark only the second season in the last decade without above-normal activity," NOAA said.
El Niño generally suppresses Atlantic hurricane activity.
El Niño is one of three phases of a climate cycle called the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). It describes natural temperature changes in the central Pacific Ocean that alter atmospheric circulation and can greatly influence global weather.
El Niño describes warmer than average water across the equatorial Pacific, while La Niña describes colder than average water conditions, and ENSO neutral refers to a state where temperatures are close to average.
During El Niño, above-average water temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean alter the position and strength of the subtropical jet stream. It's typically more robust and extends well into the Caribbean and Atlantic Ocean. The jet stream is a belt of very fast winds high in the atmosphere.
It's these strong winds that hinder tropical development in the Atlantic during an El Niño. Calm conditions are generally more conducive to hurricane formation.
When water temperatures in the El Niño zone reach at least 2 degrees Celsius above average for at least three consecutive months, it is considered a Super El Niño. These events are not as common as a typical El Niño and have a massive influence not only on the Atlantic hurricane season, but also other weather patterns around the globe.
Taken in a vacuum, the stronger the El Niño event, the more wind will be present to limit storm development in the Atlantic.
(FOX Weather)
A strong El Niño has already taken hold, with water temperatures in the El Niño zone now 2.07 degrees above average, higher than the same point for other recent Super El Niño events of 2015, 1997, 1991, and 1982.
According to NOAA, some computer forecast models suggest this El Niño could be the strongest event since record keeping began in 1950. In its July update, NOAA said El Niño could reach historically strong conditions between October and December, with a 97% chance of lasting through next spring.
However, the agency cautioned that a record-breaking El Niño event could produce atmospheric impacts never before seen.
"A strong event could have different impacts than those traditionally observed as opposed to similar impacts with greater intensity," NOAA said.
The development of El Niño this year was well forecast by NOAA and other agencies, with the main questions being how quickly it would strengthen and what intensity it would reach.
NOAA's forecast parallels Colorado State University's (CSU) August outlook, released Wednesday, which called for 9 named storms, 4 hurricanes, including 1 major (Category 3 or stronger) hurricane this year. CSU pioneered early-year hurricane season forecasts beginning in 1984.
While such a strong El Niño is expected to virtually shut down hurricane formation in the open waters of the Atlantic, it would still allow for so-called "homegrown" tropical systems in the northern Gulf and along the Southeast coast.
Although these systems tend to be weaker and shorter-lived compared to storms that develop farther out in the Atlantic, they also generally have shorter lead times before impacts occur, the FOX Forecast Center said.
Beyond the forecast, both NOAA and FOX Weather Hurricane Specialist Bryan Norcross urged people to ensure they have a hurricane plan in place, cautioning that even in seasons with fewer storms, it only takes one to create major impacts.
